title: Sweat and cooling
prompt: Sweat evaporates from your skin. What happens?
explain: Evaporation absorbs heat from the skin and surroundings.

title: A chilly test tube
prompt: A reaction makes its test tube feel colder. Consider the reacting mixture as the system.
explain: The system absorbs heat from the surrounding test tube and skin.

title: Same mass, same temperature change
prompt: Compare equal masses of water and aluminum heated by the same ΔT. Which needs more heat?
explain: Water has the greater specific heat capacity, so mcΔT is larger.

title: Temperature and energy
prompt: What does temperature measure?
choices: Total energy regardless of sample mass
explain: Temperature describes average kinetic energy, not total heat content.

title: During a plateau
prompt: What happens to temperature while a pure substance boils at fixed pressure?
explain: Heat changes the phase and intermolecular potential energy during the plateau.

title: Instant cold pack
prompt: An instant cold pack feels cold after you squeeze it and the salt dissolves. Treat the dissolving mixture as the system.
answer: Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings
choices: Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings
Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
explain: The cold feeling means heat flows from your hand into the mixture, so the process is endothermic (q > 0).

title: Chemical hand warmer
prompt: A chemical hand warmer feels hot while it reacts. Treat the reacting chemicals as the system.
answer: Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
choices: Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings
Endothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
explain: Heat leaves the reacting chemicals and warms your hands, so the reaction is exothermic (q < 0).

title: Steam burns
prompt: Steam at 100 °C usually burns skin worse than liquid water at 100 °C. What is the best explanation?
choices: Steam has a higher temperature than boiling water
Steam has no heat to give
explain: Condensation releases the heat of vaporization in addition to the heat released as the water cools.

title: Ice melting in a drink
prompt: Ice melts in a room-temperature drink. What happens to the heat the ice takes in?
answer: It breaks attractions between water molecules
choices: It breaks attractions between water molecules
explain: The heat of fusion increases the potential energy of the molecules as they move apart, not their average kinetic energy.

title: Cold metal rail
prompt: You touch a cold metal rail with a warm hand. Which way does heat flow?
answer: From your hand to the rail
choices: From your hand to the rail
From the rail to your hand
explain: Heat always flows spontaneously from the warmer object to the cooler object.

title: Water on a cold glass
prompt: Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass on a humid day. What is happening to the water vapor?
explain: Vapor to liquid is condensation, an exothermic phase change.

title: Sign of q
prompt: A system releases heat to its surroundings. What is the sign of q for the system?
explain: Energy leaving the system makes q negative.

title: Which warms faster?
prompt: The same amount of heat is added to 50 g of water and 50 g of iron. Which temperature rises more?
explain: Iron has a much smaller specific heat than water, so the same q causes a larger ΔT.

title: Freezer
prompt: Liquid water in a freezer turns into ice. What happens to energy in the water?
answer: It releases heat as it freezes
choices: It releases heat as it freezes
It absorbs heat as it freezes
explain: Freezing is exothermic: the water gives heat to the colder surroundings.

title: Coastal climate
prompt: Coastal cities often have milder temperatures than inland cities. Which property of water helps most?
explain: Water absorbs or releases a lot of heat with a small temperature change, which moderates temperature swings.

title: Cooling coffee
prompt: A hot cup of coffee cools on a desk. What is the sign of q for the coffee?
explain: Heat flows out of the coffee into the cooler surroundings, so q is negative for the coffee.

title: Dry ice
prompt: Dry ice (solid CO₂) changes directly to gas at room conditions. Which statement is correct?
choices: Sublimation is the same as freezing
explain: Solid to gas is sublimation, an endothermic phase change.

title: Rubbing alcohol
prompt: Rubbing alcohol feels cold when it evaporates from your skin. Why?
answer: Evaporation absorbs heat from the skin
choices: Evaporation absorbs heat from the skin
The alcohol is colder than ice
Evaporation releases heat to the skin
explain: Evaporating liquid takes in heat from the skin, which cools the skin.

title: Bathtub versus cup
prompt: A bathtub of 40 °C water and a cup of 90 °C water are compared. Which contains more total thermal energy?
explain: Thermal energy depends on mass as well as temperature, and the bathtub holds far more water.

title: Fusion versus vaporization
prompt: For water, which phase change needs more heat per mole at normal pressure?
explain: Vaporization (about 40.7 kJ/mol) needs far more heat than fusion (about 6.02 kJ/mol) because the attractions are separated completely.

title: Burning a candle
prompt: A candle burns and warms the air above it. Treat the burning wax as the system.
answer: Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
choices: Exothermic: releases heat to the surroundings
Endothermic: absorbs heat from the surroundings
explain: Combustion releases heat, so q is negative for the reacting system.

title: Freezing plateau
prompt: What happens to temperature while pure water freezes at fixed pressure?
explain: The released heat comes from the phase change, so the temperature stays at the freezing point until freezing is complete.

title: State function
prompt: Which quantity depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken?
explain: ΔH and ΔE are state functions. Heat and work depend on the path, although their sum ΔE = q + w does not.

title: Isolated system
prompt: A sealed, insulated, rigid container exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings. What is ΔE for the contents?
explain: With no heat or work crossing the boundary, q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔE = 0.

title: Sign of work
prompt: A gas expands against a constant external pressure. What is the sign of w for the gas?
explain: Work done BY the system lowers its energy, so w is negative. Work done ON the system is positive.

title: Constant-volume heat
prompt: A reaction is run in a rigid bomb calorimeter. The heat measured equals which quantity?
explain: At constant volume no PΔV work occurs, so qv = ΔE.

title: Constant-pressure heat
prompt: A reaction is run in an open coffee-cup calorimeter. The heat measured equals which quantity?
explain: At constant pressure qp = ΔH.

title: Reversing a reaction
prompt: A reaction has ΔH = −120 kJ. What is ΔH for the reverse reaction?
explain: Reversing a reaction changes the sign of ΔH and leaves the magnitude unchanged.

title: Standard enthalpy of an element
prompt: What is ΔHf° of an element in its standard state, such as O2(g)?
explain: Formation enthalpy is defined as zero for an element in its most stable form at standard conditions.
